recent_posts.title: Automated Security Testing with OWASP Nettacker - Sam Stepanyan - NDC Security 2026
recent_posts.summary: OWASP Nettacker is a free, open-source network security scanner written in Python that helps organizations perform automated security testing, asset discovery, and vulnerability scanning across entire networks. Unlike tools like Burp Suite or ZAP that scan a single website, Nettacker is a mass scanner capable of scanning hundreds or thousands of IP addresses, subdomains, and networks simultaneously. It features over 120 modules covering port scanning, subdomain enumeration, vulnerability detection (including CVE-specific modules), brute-force credential testing, and SSL certificate analysis. The tool includes a built-in SQLite/PostgreSQL database, a web UI, REST API, and supports CI/CD integration via GitHub Actions. Key use cases include asset inventory, detecting default credentials on IoT devices, finding exposed admin panels, identifying vulnerable software versions, and scan comparison for detecting network changes over time. It can be installed via pip, Docker, or found in Black Arch Linux.

recent_posts.title: Breaking the Black Box: Why Testing Generative AI Is Full Spectrum - Jason Ross - NDC Security 2026
recent_posts.summary: A conference talk by Jason Ross (OWASP GenAI red team lead, Salesforce) covering the fundamental differences between traditional security testing and testing generative AI systems. Key themes include: the non-deterministic, stochastic nature of LLMs making results unrepeatable; hallucinations as an inherent unfixable flaw; why black-box red teaming is largely useless for AI; the distinction between jailbreaking (attacking model guardrails) and prompt injection (attacking the application layer); indirect and cross-prompt injection via RAG databases, emails, logs, and uploaded files; specific attack techniques including crescendo attacks, context window exhaustion, CROP attacks using cultural references, adversarial suffixes, Unicode smuggling, and role-play manipulation. The talk also covers agentic system risks, the immaturity of current AI red teaming tooling, and demos of open-source tools like Garak, PyRIT, and the speaker's own Crop Duster and Tapper tools. Core message: prompt injection is an inherent, unfixable flaw — the goal is minimizing blast radius, not elimination.

recent_posts.title: OWASP Juice Shop: Take your security vitamins! - Jannik Hollenbach & Björn Kimminich
recent_posts.summary: OWASP Juice Shop is an intentionally vulnerable web application with 110+ hacking challenges covering SQL injection, XSS, and many other real-world vulnerabilities. The talk covers a live demo of the shop's normal functionality followed by demonstrations of exploiting SQL injection and XSS vulnerabilities. Key ecosystem features include: a hacking instructor for guided learning, a scoreboard, full rebranding support via YAML config, Cypress-based end-to-end tests that exploit all challenges, a Grafana monitoring dashboard, and MultiJuicer — a Kubernetes-based platform for running isolated Juice Shop instances per team in workshops. A new 3D animated globe CTF scoreboard visualization is previewed. The maintainers also discuss the growing problem of AI-generated spam pull requests threatening open source sustainability. The tech stack is Node.js/Express/Angular with SQLite, and MultiJuicer is written in Go.

recent_posts.title: It is rough without a WAF - José Carlos Chávez - NDC Security 2026
recent_posts.summary: A conference talk from NDC Security 2026 covering the role of Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) in defending against supply chain vulnerabilities. The speaker, a security engineer at Okta and maintainer of the Coraza WAF project, walks through the 2025 threat landscape: 48,000+ new CVEs, 28% of exploits launched within 24 hours of disclosure, and AI-accelerated attack weaponization. Core topics include why patching alone is insufficient (transitive dependency sprawl, ownership ambiguity, release cycle delays), how WAFs provide virtual patching and buy time for proper remediation, and the challenges of WAF deployment (false positives, rule ownership, drift over time). The talk introduces Coraza, an open-source Go-based WAF, and concludes with a forward-looking view on dynamic rules, AI-aware detection, and the need for active monitoring rather than set-and-forget WAF deployments.

recent_posts.title: Who Gave the Agent Admin Rights?! Securing Cloud & AI Machine Identities - Bodhisattva Das
recent_posts.summary: A conference talk covering the security risks of non-human identities (NHIs) — API keys, IAM roles, CI/CD tokens, AI agent credentials — and how to detect their abuse. Uses the 2019 Capital One breach as a case study showing how a misconfigured WAF, SSRF vulnerability, and overprivileged IAM role led to 100M+ records stolen. Extends the threat model to AI agents that can be manipulated via prompt injection to perform SSRF attacks against AWS IMDS. Demonstrates detection using Wazuh with 100 custom rules and 92 Sigma YAML rules covering credential discovery, cloud metadata abuse, Kubernetes security, CI/CD pipeline attacks, AI agent anomalies, and SPIFFE/SPIRE workload identity attacks. Also covers bidirectional correlation rules to catch multi-stage attack chains. Provides actionable steps: audit NHIs, enable IMDSv2, enforce least privilege, add AI agent URL allowlisting, and deploy the open-source detection rule library.

recent_posts.title: AppSec Security: The SDLC in the age of agentic - Jon Mccoy - NDC Security 2026
Protocol-Hopping C2: Transport-Agnostic Command & Control That Won't Die - Francine Solheim
recent_posts.summary: A security architect presents the concept of transport-agnostic or protocol-hopping C2 (Command & Control) infrastructure, explaining how separating the stateful command core from transport adapters allows malware to survive protocol-level blocking. The talk demonstrates how an agent can failover from HTTP to DNS to ICMP while maintaining session state and intent, warning defenders that blocking a transport protocol is containment, not eradication. Key takeaways include the need to validate host-level persistence after transport disruption, layer network and endpoint telemetry, and shift detection focus from protocol signatures to behavioral patterns like beacon periodicity and session continuity.

recent_posts.title: ¥app.alert(1) is the new alert(1): PDFs as a vector to inject JavaScript in web apps - Luigi Gubello
recent_posts.summary: A security research presentation exploring how PDF files can be used as attack vectors to inject JavaScript into web applications. Covers two XSS vulnerabilities in PDF.js (CVE-2018-5158 and a 2024 CVE), both caused by improperly sanitized arrays. Also examines Apryse/PDFTron SDK vulnerabilities where a JavaScript sandbox implemented in pure JavaScript was bypassed using the delete operator to restore blocked browser APIs. Demonstrates a real-world RCE chain in the LogSeq Electron app via an outdated PDF.js version. Discusses why simple app.alert(1) proofs-of-concept are insufficient for PDF-based XSS reports, and recommends mitigations including strict CSP with hashes/nonces, isolated subdomains for PDF rendering, and disabling embedded JavaScript support when not needed.

recent_posts.title: From WAN to NAS: A Pwn2Own Journey Through the SOHO Attack Surface - Daan Keuper - NDC Security 2026
recent_posts.summary: A detailed walkthrough of a Pwn2Own IoT competition entry targeting a SOHO attack chain: compromising a QNAP router from the WAN side and pivoting to a TrueNAS Mini X on the LAN. The talk covers the full research process including target selection, firmware decryption, attack surface enumeration (outgoing connections, listening services, IPv6 exposure), and the vulnerabilities ultimately exploited. On the NAS side, a Python-based jail manager (iocage) used an unsafe tarfile.extractall call over HTTP, enabling a DNS-spoofing/MITM attack to overwrite the user database. On the router, a DNS lookup for localhost's AAAA record led to discovery of an internal gRPC service; by impersonating the cloud agent, an address6 field in a site.json config was passed unsanitized to a shell, yielding root code execution. The talk emphasizes failed approaches, heap shaping challenges, and the realities of competing seventh out of seven teams — yet all vulnerabilities were confirmed as previously unknown zero-days.

recent_posts.title: Attacking AI - Jason Haddix - NDC Security 2026
recent_posts.summary: A conference talk by Jason Haddix covering offensive security methodology for AI systems. Drawing on 2+ years of AI pentesting experience, it walks through a custom LLM assessment methodology covering input identification, ecosystem attacks, prompt engineering leakage, RAG data exfiltration, and pivoting to internal systems. Real-world case studies include bypassing Amazon Rufus guardrails via ASCII encoding, exfiltrating system prompts and API keys from healthcare and automotive enterprise AI systems, and attacking a SIEM vendor's AI integration. The talk introduces a Metasploit-inspired taxonomy of prompt injection techniques (intents, techniques, evasions, utilities), demonstrates tools like Parcel Tongue for evasion generation, and provides resources including 23+ practice labs, bug bounty programs, and CTF competitions for learning AI red teaming.
